questions.q: How does `HashMap` find the bucket for a key?
o: It spreads `hashCode()` and maps it to an array index
It compares the key with every stored entry in turn
It sorts the keys and then uses binary search
It converts the key to a string and indexes by its length
questions.w: Index is derived from the hash (roughly `(n - 1) & hash`). Within the bucket, `equals()` picks the exact key.

questions.q: Two different keys land in the same bucket. What is this called, and how is it handled?
o: A collision; entries chain in a list or tree inside the bucket
A conflict; the second key replaces the first one
An overflow; the map throws an exception
A mismatch; the map rehashes both keys forever
questions.w: Since Java 8 a long chain (8 or more entries, table big enough) is converted to a red-black tree, so the worst case is O(log n).

questions.q: You use a mutable object as a key and change a field used in `hashCode()` after inserting it. What happens on `get()`?
o: The lookup probably misses, because the entry sits in the old bucket
The map moves the entry to its new bucket on its own
The map throws `ConcurrentModificationException`
The lookup still works because the reference is the same
questions.w: Keys should be effectively immutable, like `String`, `Integer` or records.

o: Equal objects must return the same hash code
Objects with the same hash code must be equal
Unequal objects must return different hash codes
`hashCode()` must return the object's memory address
questions.w: Equal hashes with unequal objects are allowed (collisions). Equal objects with different hashes break the map.

o: When size passes capacity times the 0.75 load factor
As soon as any bucket holds more than one entry
Every time a new entry is added
Only when `rehash()` is called by hand
questions.w: Resizing doubles the table and redistributes entries, which is costly. Pre-size the map when you know the entry count.

questions.q: Is `HashMap` safe for concurrent updates from several threads?
o: No; use `ConcurrentHashMap` or synchronise externally
Yes; every operation is locked inside the class
Yes, but only for read operations
Yes, provided the keys are all strings
questions.w: Concurrent writes can lose entries or corrupt the structure. Reads during a write may also see inconsistent state.

questions.q: What is the average time complexity of `get()` and `put()` in a well-distributed `HashMap`?
o: O(n)
O(log n) always
O(n log n)
questions.w: Constant on average. A bad `hashCode()` that clusters keys degrades towards O(n) or O(log n) with tree bins.

questions.q: What does `HashMap` do with a `null` key?
o: It allows one `null` key, kept in bucket 0
It throws `NullPointerException` at once
It ignores the call without any error
It stores the key in a separate sorted list
questions.w: `HashMap` allows one `null` key and many `null` values. `ConcurrentHashMap` and `Hashtable` reject both.
